newsitem.title: CHINA: China bans violators from securities industry.
newsitem.headline: China bans violators from securities industry.

text.p: China on Tuesday issued new rules banning people found to have engaged in serious securities irregularities from the industry in a move to further strengthen supervision of the markets, analysts said.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) rules said that company officials found to have engaged in insider trading and traders found to have rigged prices will be banned from the industry permanently or at least for several years.
A similar ban will also be imposed on accountants and lawyers found to have collaborated with the violators under the rules, published in the Shanghai Securities News.

"Violators found guilty by the CSRC will be banned from assuming senior positions in listed firms or from trading on the securities markets permanently or at least for a few years," said the CSRC, China's top securities watchdog, said.
The rules, part of a significant tightening of supervision of the securities industry put into force from late last year, took immediate effect.

In recent months, the CSRC has publicly criticised and punished branches of all major Chinese banks and securities houses for irregularities such as the use of credit to buy shares on both the primary and secondary markets.
The China Securities newspaper quoted a CSRC spokesman as saying the new rules were intended to further standardise the markets and protect the interests of retail investors.
Industry sources generally welcomed the new rules. Some said the announcement was timed to once again cool the stock markets.
"The CSRC has chosen this moment to issue the rules because there have been signs of over-heating in the markets since the death of (Chinese leader) Deng Xiaoping," said a stock analyst.

The markets had expected Deng's death to have a significant negative impact, but stock prices have risen nearly every day since his death on February 19, largely due to indications that post-Deng China will be politically stable, analysts said.
Most traders and retail investors believe 1997 will be a good year for the markets due to China's improving economy and Hong Kong's return to Beijing rule in July.
An editorial in the Shanghai Securities News said the new rules would help to clean up the markets.
"China's young securities markets include many immature elements," it said. "There is an urgent need to rein in the horses leading the herd in the wrong direction."
The China Securities newspaper said in an editorial that severe punishments were needed to check illegal trading.

"It is necessary to severely punish rule violators to standardise the markets," it said. "The new rules mean that anybody who does not play by the rules will now be permanently purged from the markets."

The rules bar listed firms and securities houses from appointing banned individuals as senior officials. Local securities authorities also must cooperate with the central government to ensure banned individuals do not continue to operate in the markets.
